claim: Classical views of cerebellar learning have suggested that the cerebellum predominantly operates according to an error-based supervised learning rule to refine movements.
source: While classical views of cerebellar learning have suggested that this structure predominantly operates according to an error-based supervised learning rule to refine movements, emerging evidence suggests that the cerebellum may also harness a wider range of learning rules to contribute to a variety of behaviors, including cognitive processes.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical perspective on cerebellar learning, representing established views in the field.

claim: Emerging evidence suggests that the cerebellum may harness a wider range of learning rules to contribute to a variety of behaviors, including cognitive processes.
source: While classical views of cerebellar learning have suggested that this structure predominantly operates according to an error-based supervised learning rule to refine movements, emerging evidence suggests that the cerebellum may also harness a wider range of learning rules to contribute to a variety of behaviors, including cognitive processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from recent studies discussed in the manuscript.

claim: A key operating principle of the brain is to establish internally generated predictions that can be compared against feedback from the external world in order to guide anticipatory actions and perceptions.
source: Across sensory and motor systems, growing evidence suggests that a key operating principle of the brain is to establish internally generated predictions that can be compared against feedback from the external world in order to guide anticipatory actions and perceptions (Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018.

claim: The cerebellum has long been thought to operate predictively to support motor control and motor learning.
source: The cerebellum has long been thought to operate predictively to support motor control and motor learning (Wolpert et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wolpert et al., 1998.

claim: The cerebellum is hypothesized to utilize a predictive model that anticipates the expected outcome of motor commands in order to refine future movements.
source: As originally proposed by Masao Ito, the cerebellum is hypothesized to utilize a predictive model that anticipates the expected outcome of motor commands in order to refine future movements (Ito, 1970; Ito, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ito, 1970 and Ito, 1972.

claim: Decades of research have provided considerable support for the hypothesis that the cerebellum utilizes a predictive model.
source: Indeed, decades of research have provided considerable support for this hypothesis (Ohyama et al., 2003), and revealed many of the circuit pathways (Apps and Garwicz, 2005) and mechanisms (Carey, 2011) that allow the cerebellum to predictively modify motor output.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ohyama et al., 2003, Apps and Garwicz, 2005, and Carey, 2011.

claim: Emerging evidence suggests that the role of the cerebellum in motor control may be more complex than previously appreciated.
source: However, emerging evidence suggests that the role of the cerebellum in motor control may be more complex than previously appreciated (Medina, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Medina, 2019.

claim: The cerebellum plays a much wider role in brain function than simply refining movements.
source: Moreover, it has also become clear that the cerebellum plays a much wider role in brain function than simply refining movements (Buckner, 2013; Leiner et al., 1986; Schmahmann, 1991; Sokolov et al., 2017; Strick et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buckner, 2013; Leiner et al., 1986; Schmahmann, 1991; Sokolov et al., 2017; Strick et al., 2009.

claim: To refine movements based on the predicted sensory consequences of action, the cerebellum must solve a credit assignment problem.
source: To refine movements based on the predicted the sensory consequences of action, the cerebellum must solve a credit assignment problem.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the computational problem the cerebellum must solve.

claim: The cerebellum must attribute deviations between actual and expected sensorimotor feedback to features of movement that occurred in the recent past.
source: Specifically, it must attribute deviations between actual and expected sensorimotor feedback to features of movement that occurred in the recent past.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the credit assignment problem.

claim: Classical models of cerebellar function argue that the credit assignment problem is solved through a supervised learning rule instructed by climbing fibers.
source: Classical models of cerebellar function argue that this problem is solved through a supervised learning rule instructed by inputs to the cerebellar cortex called climbing fibers (CFs, Figure 1; Albus, 1971; Marr, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Albus, 1971 and Marr, 1969, and references Figure 1.

claim: Supervised learning is characterized by teaching signals that can report whether or not expectations match outcomes.
source: Supervised learning is characterized by teaching signals that can report whether or not expectations match outcomes (i.e. a yes or no signal).
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge about supervised learning.

claim: Climbing fibers are thought to instruct learning by signaling the occurrence of movement errors.
source: In the cerebellum, CFs are thought to instruct learning by signaling the occurrence of movement errors.
evidence: This is a statement about the classical model of CF function.

claim: Error signals from climbing fibers are thought to correct future movement by generating large dendritic calcium spikes (complex spikes) in Purkinje cells.
source: These error signals are thought to correct future movement by generating large dendritic calcium spikes (so-called complex spikes, Cspks) in the output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism by which CFs are thought to instruct learning.

claim: Complex spikes can produce heterosynaptic plasticity on preceding inputs from the mossy fiber to granule cell pathway.
source: In turn, Cspks can produce heterosynaptic plasticity on preceding inputs from another pathway, the mossy fiber (MF) to granule cell pathway.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of cerebellar learning.

claim: The mossy fiber pathway carries contextual information necessary for learning.
source: Because the MF pathway carries contextual information necessary for learning, such a plasticity rule has long been thought to provide a key substrate for generating cerebellar-dependent supervised motor learning.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of the mossy fiber pathway in classical models.

claim: Climbing fibers originate in the inferior olive and excite Purkinje cell dendrites.
source: Climbing fibers originate in the inferior olive (IO), and excite (plus signs) Purkinje cell dendrites.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Climbing fiber inputs serve to instruct heterosynaptic plasticity at synapses from the mossy fiber pathway.
source: These inputs serve to instruct heterosynaptic plasticity at synapses from the mossy fiber pathway, an excitatory pathway that originates in the pontine nuclei and elsewhere.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The mossy fiber pathway originates in the pontine nuclei and elsewhere.
source: These inputs serve to instruct heterosynaptic plasticity at synapses from the mossy fiber pathway, an excitatory pathway that originates in the pontine nuclei and elsewhere.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The mossy fiber pathway excites granule cells and terminates in excitatory parallel fiber inputs onto Purkinje cells.
source: The mossy fiber pathway excites granule cells, and terminates in excitatory parallel fiber inputs onto Purkinje cells.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Purkinje cells are inhibitory and regulate the activity of output neurons in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Purkinje cells are inhibitory (minus sign), and regulate the activity of output neurons in the cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The supervised learning rule works well to describe cerebellar activity in the climbing fiber and mossy fiber pathways during many behaviors.
source: This supervised learning rule works well to describe cerebellar activity in the CF and MF pathways during many behaviors, and provides a compelling model to explain how the cerebellum can modify certain movements.
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of the supervised learning model.

claim: Supervised learning requires that climbing fibers have access to a complete menu of erroneous actions in order to provide accurate error-based feedback.
source: However, such supervised learning also requires that CFs have access to a complete menu of erroneous actions in order to provide accurate error-based feedback.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements of supervised learning.

claim: The supervised learning rule is ideal when there is a yoked relationship between stimulus and action.
source: In other words, this supervised learning rule is ideal when there is a yoked relationship between stimulus and action, as is common for many well-studied cerebellar-dependent behaviors.
evidence: This is a logical inference about when supervised learning is most applicable.

claim: In eyelid conditioning, animals learn to associate a neutral sensory stimulus with a delayed corneal airpuff that produces a reflexive eyelid closure.
source: In this behavior, animals learn to associate a neutral sensory stimulus with a delayed corneal airpuff that produces a reflexive eyelid closure.
evidence: This is a description of the eyelid conditioning paradigm.

claim: Climbing fibers can accurately instruct a predictive eyelid closure according to the principles of supervised learning by responding via a hardwired neural pathway from the sensory periphery to the corneal airpuff.
source: By responding via a hardwired neural pathway from the sensory periphery to the same corneal airpuff that produces a reflexive blink, CFs can accurately instruct a predictive eyelid closure according to the principles of supervised learning (Kim and Thompson, 1997; Medina et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim and Thompson, 1997 and Medina et al., 2000.

claim: It has been challenging to understand how a supervised learning rule could provide an effective means for learning in more complex motor behaviors without a fixed stimulus-action relationship.
source: In more complex motor behaviors without a fixed stimulus-action relationship, as well as many non-motor behaviors, it has been challenging to understand how such a supervised learning rule could provide an effective means for learning.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the supervised learning model.

claim: During arbitrary visuomotor reaching tasks, climbing fiber-driven complex spikes in Purkinje cells have been shown to reflect predictive signals that are not consistent with motor errors.
source: For example, during arbitrary visuomotor reaching tasks, CF-driven Cspks in Purkinje cells have been shown to reflect predictive signals that are not consistent with motor errors (Kitazawa et al., 1998; Streng et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kitazawa et al., 1998 and Streng et al., 2017.

claim: Complex spikes can be predictive of task parameters such as reach destination, upcoming movement kinematics, or future position errors.
source: Instead, these studies have shown that Cspks can be predictive of task parameters such as reach destination, upcoming movement kinematics, or future position errors.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the studies cited in the previous sentence.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that the cerebellum may be able to harness a wider range of distinct learning rules to modify behavior during eyelid conditioning.
source: Even during eyelid conditioning, recent evidence suggests that the cerebellum may be able to harness a wider range of distinct learning rules to modify behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about emerging evidence, supported by inference from subsequent discussion.

claim: Ohmae and Medina demonstrated that climbing fibers could provide a learning signal that meets the criteria described by temporal-difference models of reinforcement learning.
source: By recording from the cerebella of awake mice locomoting on a treadmill during eyelid conditioning, the authors demonstrated that CFs could provide a different type of learning signal; namely, one that meets the criteria described by temporal-difference (TD) models of reinforcement learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the Ohmae and Medina study.

claim: In temporal-difference learning, teaching signals are scalar and vary according to current expectations.
source: Specifically, in TD learning, teaching signals are scalar, and vary according to current expectations.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge about TD learning, supported by citation to Sutton and Barto, 1998.

claim: Climbing fiber activity met the criterion of temporal-difference learning, as complex spikes were more probable in response to an unexpected unconditioned stimulus than when the same stimulus was expected.
source: Indeed, the authors found that CF activity met this criterion, as Cspks were more probable in response to an unconditioned stimulus (US; i.e. corneal airpuff) that was unexpected than when the same stimulus was expected (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Ohmae and Medina's study, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The probability of complex spikes on unexpected US trials was higher than for expected US trials where no conditioned response was generated, suggesting that differences in sensory encoding of the US were not responsible for the differences in complex spike probability.
source: Importantly, the probability of Cspks on unexpected US trials was higher than for expected US trials where no conditioned response (CR) was generated, suggesting that differences in sensory encoding of the US were not responsible for the differences in Cspk probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Ohmae and Medina's study and logical inference.

claim: These findings contradict what would be predicted by a supervised learning model, which would suggest the same complex spike probability on any trial type without a predictive eyelid closure.
source: These findings hence contradict what would be predicted by a supervised learning model, which would instead suggest the same Cspk probability on any trial type without a predictive eyelid closure to block the aversive corneal airpuff.
evidence: This is a logical inference comparing the data to predictions of the supervised learning model.

claim: In temporal-difference learning models, teaching signals are modulated by experience to represent higher-order reinforcing stimuli.
source: Another key feature of TD learning models is that teaching signals are modulated by experience to represent higher-order reinforcing stimuli.
evidence: This is a statement about TD learning models based on established knowledge.

claim: Climbing fiber activity met the criterion of representing higher-order reinforcing stimuli, as complex spikes emerged in response to the conditioned stimulus after learning.
source: Again, CF activity met this criterion, as Cspks emerged in response to the conditioned stimulus (CS; i.e. an LED that reliably preceded the airpuff) after learning (Figure 2) (See also ten Brinke et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Ohmae and Medina's study, illustrated in Figure 2, and a citation to ten Brinke et al., 2015.

claim: Complex spikes are more probable in response to an unexpected unconditioned stimulus (corneal airpuff) than when the same stimulus is expected.
source: CF-driven Cspks, recorded here after learning, are more probable in response to a US (corneal airpuff) that is unexpected (black) than when the same stimulus is expected (red).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Complex spikes follow the conditioned stimulus after learning and are reduced below baseline levels when the expected unconditioned stimulus does not occur.
source: Cspks also follow the conditioned stimulus after learning, and are reduced below baseline levels when the expected US does not occur.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The properties of teaching signals in temporal-difference models (scalar responses based on expectation and learned responses to higher-order reinforcing stimuli) allow the system to learn by trial-and-error exploration without the need for prior knowledge about a correct outcome.
source: In TD models however, these properties of teaching signals (scalar responses based on expectation and learned responses to higher-order reinforcing stimuli) allow the system to learn by trial-and-error exploration without the need for prior knowledge about a correct outcome (e.g. the final, correctly-executed learned movement).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of TD learning based on established knowledge.

claim: The properties of temporal-difference learning may be ideal to enable a cerebellar contribution to learning across a range of motor and non-motor behaviors, particularly behaviors where learning is guided by predictions about upcoming reward.
source: Such properties may be ideal to enable a cerebellar contribution to learning across a range of motor and non-motor behaviors, and in particular behaviors where learning is guided by predictions about upcoming reward.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of TD learning in the cerebellum.

claim: The neural seat of reward-guided reinforcement learning has historically been considered to be the striatum, where projections from VTA dopamine neurons largely obey the principles of temporal-difference models.
source: The neural seat of reward-guided reinforcement learning has historically been considered to be the striatum, where projections from VTA dopamine neurons largely obey the principles of TD models to instruct synaptic plasticity and learning about reward-predictive events (Glimcher, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Glimcher, 2011.

claim: Recent work has provided compelling evidence that the cerebellum may also contribute to reward-based reinforcement learning.
source: Recent work has provided compelling evidence that the cerebellum may also contribute to reward-based reinforcement learning (Heffley and Hull, 2019; Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019; Larry et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heffley and Hull, 2019; Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019; Larry et al., 2019.

claim: Two studies using calcium imaging demonstrated that climbing fibers can exhibit responses that are consistent with reward-based reinforcement learning signals.
source: For example, two studies using calcium imaging to visualize Cspk activity in awake mice during operant learning tasks have now demonstrated that CFs can exhibit responses that are consistent with reward-based reinforcement learning signals (Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heffley et al., 2018 and Kostadinov et al., 2019, and references Figure 3.

claim: Complex spikes also report violated expectations by signaling when an expected reward is not delivered.
source: In addition, these studies found that Cspks also report violated expectations by signaling when an expected reward is not delivered (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the studies by Heffley et al., 2018 and Kostadinov et al., 2019, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Mice were trained to press and release a lever as instructed by a visual cue in order to receive reward.
source: Left, mice were trained to press and release a lever as instructed by a visual cue in order to receive reward.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental paradigm shown in Figure 3.

claim: Complex spike activity was greatest for lever releases that predicted reward delivery.
source: Middle, Cspk activity was greatest for lever releases that predicted reward delivery.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Complex spike activity was enhanced when expected reward was not delivered.
source: Right, Cspk activity was enhanced when expected reward was not delivered.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The results showing complex spike activity in response to movements that result in reward are not only consistent with reinforcement learning, but directly oppose the motor error hypothesis of climbing fiber activity.
source: These results are not only consistent with reinforcement learning, but directly oppose the motor error hypothesis of CF activity.
evidence: This is a logical inference comparing the data to the motor error hypothesis.

claim: Complex spike activity was generated in response to actions or events that accurately predicted upcoming reward, which necessarily occurred when animals correctly executed movements rather than when movement was mis-executed.
source: Specifically, because Cspk activity was generated in response to actions or events that accurately predicted upcoming reward (Heffley et al., 2018), this activity necessarily occurred when animals correctly executed movements rather than when movement was mis-executed.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the data presented in Heffley et al., 2018.

claim: It initially appears paradoxical that climbing fiber learning signals should occur in response to movements that result in reward and thus do not immediately require modification.
source: It initially appears paradoxical that CF learning signals should occur in response to movements that result in reward, and thus do not immediately require modification.
evidence: This is a statement about the apparent paradox in the data.

claim: The reward-predictive complex spike responses associated with movement occurred in the learned condition, when the expectation that a specific movement or event would result in reward had already been established.
source: However, it is important to note that the reward-predictive Cspk responses associated with movement in these studies occurred in the learned condition, when the expectation that a specific movement or event would result in reward had already been established.
evidence: This is a clarification about the timing of the observed responses.

claim: At the timepoint when reward-predictive complex spike responses occur, reinforcement learning principles suggest that complex spikes should be used to drive second order conditioning.
source: At this timepoint, reinforcement learning principles suggest that Cspks should be used to drive second order conditioning (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a prediction based on reinforcement learning theory, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: If a new stimulus and/or action emerged that reliably provided an even earlier predictor of reward, climbing fiber-driven signals would be ideally situated to drive a higher order learned association to that new event.
source: In other words, if a new stimulus and/or action emerged that reliably provided an even earlier predictor of reward, these CF-driven signals would be ideally situated to drive a higher order learned association to that new event.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on reinforcement learning theory.

claim: Before learning, climbing fibers are driven by an unexpected unconditioned stimulus.
source: Before learning, CFs are driven by an unexpected US.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: After learning, climbing fibers are driven by a conditioned stimulus that accurately predicts the unconditioned stimulus (CS1).
source: After learning, CFs are driven by a CS that accurately predicts the US (CS1).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: If a new conditioned stimulus occurs earlier in time (CS2), climbing fiber activity can then be driven by this higher order stimulus.
source: If a new CS occurs earlier in time (CS2), CF activity can then be driven by this higher order stimulus.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: If the expected unconditioned stimulus is omitted, climbing fiber activity is reduced (negative prediction error), serving to extinguish associations with the no longer appropriate CS1 and CS2.
source: Finally, if the expected US is omitted, CF activity is reduced (negative prediction error), serving to extinguish associations with the no longer appropriate CS1 and CS2.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Such a mechanism could enable the association of multiple actions in order to establish a fully coordinated movement.
source: Such a mechanism could enable the association of multiple actions in order to establish a fully coordinated movement.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential function of higher-order conditioning.

claim: Cerebellar-dependent sequence learning has been demonstrated only when movement feedback signals are reinforced by exogenously stimulated climbing fiber activity.
source: To date, cerebellar-dependent sequence learning has been demonstrated only when movement feedback signals are reinforced by exogenously stimulated CF activity (Khilkevich et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Khilkevich et al., 2018.

claim: It remains to be tested whether learned climbing fiber responses to conditioned stimuli can in fact support higher order conditioning and/or motor sequence learning.
source: However, it remains to be tested whether learned CF responses to conditioned stimuli can in fact support higher order conditioning and/or motor sequence learning.
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in the field.

claim: It remains plausible that learned climbing fiber responses to conditioned stimuli can allow further modification of movement by other means, for example by directly modulating the activity of cerebellar nuclei neurons.
source: It also remains plausible that learned CF responses to conditioned stimuli can allow further modification of movement by other means, for example by directly modulating the activity of CbN neurons (Ten Brinke et al., 2019; Ten Brinke et al., 2017), or may serve a different purpose altogether by enabling cerebellar output to downstream brain regions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to Ten Brinke et al., 2019 and Ten Brinke et al., 2017.

claim: While the complex spike signals reported in Heffley et al. and Kostadinov et al. are consistent with reinforcement learning, they contrast in key ways with the complex spike patterns described by Ohmae and Medina.
source: Interestingly, while the Cspk signals reported in both Heffley et al. and Kostadinov et al. are consistent with reinforcement learning, they contrast in key ways with the Cspk patterns described by Ohmae and Medina.
evidence: This is a comparison of results across different studies.

claim: Neither Heffley et al. nor Kostadinov et al. observed a decrease in complex spike activity when expected reward was not delivered.
source: In particular, neither Heffley et al. nor Kostadinov et al. observed a decrease in Cspk activity when expected reward was not delivered.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings of Heffley et al. and Kostadinov et al.

claim: Both Heffley et al. and Kostadinov et al. reported elevated complex spike activity in response to defied expectations.
source: Instead, both studies reported elevated Cspk activity in response to defied expectations.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings of Heffley et al. and Kostadinov et al.

claim: The elevated complex spike responses shown by Heffley et al. and Kostadinov et al. are consistent with unsigned prediction errors, but not with the types of signed prediction errors typically associated with temporal-difference learning.
source: Such responses are consistent with unsigned prediction errors, but not with the types of signed prediction errors typically associated with TD learning (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a comparison of the data to TD learning theory.

claim: The decreases in complex spike activity demonstrated by Ohmae et al. are ideal to promote extinction learning during eyeblink conditioning when the aversive conditioned stimulus is absent.
source: The decreases in Cspk activity demonstrated by Ohmae et al. are ideal to promote extinction learning during eyeblink conditioning when the aversive conditioned stimulus is absent (Medina et al., 2002), and may therefore also be a hallmark of behaviors with fixed stimulus-action relationships.
evidence: This is an inference about the function of decreased Cspk activity, supported by a citation to Medina et al., 2002.

claim: The increased complex spike responses shown by Heffley et al. and Kostadinov et al. may promote exploration and new associations during behavior that requires flexible stimulus-action relationships.
source: In contrast, the increased Cspk responses shown by Heffley et al. and Kostadinov et al. may promote exploration and new associations during behavior that requires flexible stimulus-action relationships.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the function of increased Cspk activity.

claim: Despite the commonality of learned complex spike responses to higher-order reinforcing stimuli across studies, it remains to be determined how specific task requirements and location within the cerebellum determine the climbing fiber response to violated expectations.
source: Hence, despite the commonality of learned Cspk responses to higher-order reinforcing stimuli across studies, it remains to be determined how specific task requirements and location within the cerebellum determine the CF response to violated expectations.
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in the field.

claim: The axons that form climbing fibers originate from neurons in the inferior olive.
source: The axons that form CFs originate from neurons in the inferior olive (IO).
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical fact.

claim: In many cerebellar-dependent behaviors, input to the inferior olive that drives climbing fibers and learning comes directly from the sensory periphery.
source: In many cerebellar-dependent behaviors, input to the IO that drives CFs and learning comes directly from the sensory periphery.
evidence: This is a statement about the sources of IO input.

claim: In eyelid conditioning, the corneal airpuff used as a US is transmitted to the inferior olive via the trigeminal ganglion, reliably triggering climbing fiber input to the cerebellum.
source: For example, in eyelid conditioning, the corneal airpuff used as a US is transmitted to the IO via the trigeminal ganglion (Kubo et al., 2018; Swenson and Castro, 1983; Van Ham and Yeo, 1992), reliably triggering CF input to the cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kubo et al., 2018; Swenson and Castro, 1983; Van Ham and Yeo, 1992.

claim: The 'hardwired' pathway from the sensory periphery to the inferior olive allows climbing fibers to respond with high fidelity in a manner consistent with supervised learning based on the causal association between stimulus and movement.
source: This 'hardwired' pathway allows CFs to respond with high fidelity in a manner consistent with supervised learning based on the causal association between stimulus and movement.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the function of the hardwired pathway.

claim: The inferior olive also receives indirect input from both cortical and subcortical brain regions that may allow it to generate more complex teaching signals than can be produced by salient sensory input from the environment.
source: However, the IO also receives indirect input from both cortical and subcortical brain regions that may allow it to generate more complex teaching signals than can be produced by salient sensory input from the environment (Ten Brinke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ten Brinke et al., 2019.

claim: One key source of input to the inferior olive is the mesodiencephalic junction.
source: One such key source of input to the IO is the mesodiencephalic junction (MDJ) (De Zeeuw et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to De Zeeuw et al., 1998.

claim: The mesodiencephalic junction is composed of multiple nuclei, some of which integrate cerebellar nuclei output and project to either downstream neurons in the spinal cord or the inferior olive.
source: This region of the midbrain is composed of multiple nuclei, some of which integrate cerebellar CbN output and project to either downstream neurons in the spinal cord (Keifer and Houk, 1994) or the IO (Onodera, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Keifer and Houk, 1994 and Onodera, 1984.

claim: Cerebellar learning has been shown to produce new mossy fiber collaterals in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Because cerebellar learning has been shown to produce new mossy fiber collaterals in the CbN (Boele et al., 2013; Kleim et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2015; Weeks et al., 2007), it has been speculated that such collaterals may convey information about learned conditioned stimuli to the MDJ, and in turn to the IO (Ten Brinke et al., 2019; Ten Brinke et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boele et al., 2013; Kleim et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2015; Weeks et al., 2007.

claim: It has been speculated that new mossy fiber collaterals in the cerebellar nuclei may convey information about learned conditioned stimuli to the mesodiencephalic junction, and in turn to the inferior olive.
source: Because cerebellar learning has been shown to produce new mossy fiber collaterals in the CbN (Boele et al., 2013; Kleim et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2015; Weeks et al., 2007), it has been speculated that such collaterals may convey information about learned conditioned stimuli to the MDJ, and in turn to the IO (Ten Brinke et al., 2019; Ten Brinke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to Ten Brinke et al., 2019 and Ten Brinke et al., 2017.

claim: In the model where mossy fiber collaterals convey learned information to the inferior olive, mossy fiber pathways carrying learned information about conditioned stimuli could be indirectly translated to the inferior olive via new collaterals, producing instructive reinforcement learning signals in climbing fibers.
source: In this model, mossy fiber pathways carrying learned information about conditioned stimuli could be indirectly translated to the IO via these new collaterals, producing instructive reinforcement learning signals in CFs.
evidence: This is a speculative model about how reinforcement learning signals might be generated.

claim: Such an extended polysynaptic pathway may partly explain why climbing fiber signals related to conditioned stimuli tend to have longer latencies than the US-related climbing fiber signals that are translated more directly from the sensory periphery.
source: Notably, such an extended polysynaptic pathway may partly explain why CF signals related to conditioned stimuli tend to have longer latencies than the US-related CF signals that are translated more directly from the sensory periphery.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of the polysynaptic pathway.

claim: The mesodiencephalic junction also integrates descending input from sources that include cortical pyramidal tract neurons.
source: The MDJ also integrates descending input from sources that include cortical pyramidal tract neurons (Veazey and Severin, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Veazey and Severin, 1982.

claim: Descending input from cortical pyramidal tract neurons likely allows the inferior olive to represent higher order cortical computations, and is therefore a good candidate to transmit the types of reward prediction and temporal-difference learning signals that have been shown recently.
source: Such input likely allows the IO to represent higher order cortical computations, and is therefore a good candidate to transmit the types of reward prediction and TD-learning signals that have been shown recently.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the function of cortical input to the IO.

claim: The inferior olive also receives inhibitory input and contains some local interneurons, raising the possibility that local computations may also enrich the repertoire of climbing fiber responses.
source: The IO also receives inhibitory input, and contains some local interneurons, raising the possibility that local computations may also enrich the repertoire of CF responses (De Zeeuw et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to De Zeeuw et al., 1998.

claim: The inferior olive receives inhibitory input from the cerebellar nuclei.
source: For example, the IO receives inhibitory input from the cerebellar nuclei (CbN) (Bengtsson and Hesslow, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bengtsson and Hesslow, 2006.

claim: Inhibitory projections from the cerebellar nuclei to the inferior olive participate in extinction learning.
source: These inhibitory projections participate in extinction learning (Medina et al., 2002), but could also play a role in gating CF activity or sculpting responses to incoming excitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Medina et al., 2002.

claim: Inhibitory inputs from the cerebellar nuclei to the inferior olive could play a role in gating climbing fiber activity or sculpting responses to incoming excitation.
source: These inhibitory projections participate in extinction learning (Medina et al., 2002), but could also play a role in gating CF activity or sculpting responses to incoming excitation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of inhibitory inputs.

claim: Inhibitory inputs could decouple stimulus-action relationships resulting from peripheral inferior olive inputs, enabling other pathways to dominate when learning requires information from other sources.
source: For example, inhibitory inputs could decouple stimulus-action relationships resulting from peripheral IO inputs, enabling other pathways to dominate when learning requires information from other sources.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of inhibitory inputs.

claim: Multiple studies have found that climbing fiber activity exhibits context dependence, and that sensory responses can be actively suppressed under certain behavioral conditions.
source: Indeed, multiple studies have found that CF activity exhibits context dependence, and that sensory responses can be actively suppressed under certain behavioral conditions (Apps, 1999; Apps and Lee, 1999; Gellman et al., 1985; Horn et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Apps, 1999; Apps and Lee, 1999; Gellman et al., 1985; Horn et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1987.

claim: Whether inhibitory cerebellar nuclei projections play a role in context-dependent inferior olive suppression remains unclear.
source: Whether inhibitory CbN projections play a role in such context-dependent IO suppression remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in the field.

claim: It has remained challenging to establish any clear predictions about the influence of discrete pathways in generating climbing fiber learning signals, as there remains an incomplete description of inputs to the inferior olive.
source: More broadly, it has remained challenging to establish any clear predictions about the influence of discrete pathways in generating CF learning signals, as there remains an incomplete description of inputs to the IO, as well as a limited understanding of when different pathways are active and how the IO integrates input to generate CF responses in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the current limitations in understanding IO function.

claim: A key step in understanding how climbing fibers can produce complex teaching signals such as those necessary for reinforcement learning will be to establish a more detailed map of input to the inferior olive, and to measure the behavioral contexts under which specific input pathways recruit climbing fiber activity.
source: Thus, a key step in understanding how CFs can produce complex teaching signals such as those necessary for reinforcement learning will be to establish a more detailed map of input to the IO, and to measure the behavioral contexts under which specific input pathways recruit CF activity.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: To mediate cerebellar learning, the teaching signals carried by climbing fibers are thought to instruct heterosynaptic plasticity at excitatory synapses from granule cells onto Purkinje cells.
source: To mediate cerebellar learning, the teaching signals carried by CFs are thought to instruct heterosynaptic plasticity at excitatory synapses from granule cells onto Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the classical model of cerebellar learning.

claim: The information carried by granule cells crucially determines what the cerebellum can learn.
source: Thus, the information carried by granule cells crucially determines what the cerebellum can learn.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the importance of granule cell representations.

claim: Classical models of the granule cell layer suggest that it serves a key role in pattern separation by expanding, sparsifying and decorrelating cerebellar input in order to maximize the number of unique representations that can be learned by Purkinje cells.
source: Classical models of the granule cell layer suggest that it serves a key role in pattern separation by expanding, sparsifying and decorrelating cerebellar input in order to maximize the number of unique representations that can be learned by Purkinje cells (Albus, 1971; Marr, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Albus, 1971 and Marr, 1969.

claim: The sheer number of granule cells makes sparse coding models appealing, as these neurons are by far the most numerous in the brain, and significantly outnumber their presynaptic mossy fiber inputs.
source: Indeed, the sheer number of granule cells makes sparse coding models appealing, as these neurons are by far the most numerous in the brain, and significantly outnumber their presynaptic mossy fiber inputs (Eccles et al., 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eccles et al., 1967.

claim: Granule cell activity has been thought to be kept sparse by synaptic inhibition, which reduces the threshold and gain of granule cell responses to incoming mossy fiber input.
source: Their activity has also been thought to be kept sparse by synaptic inhibition, which reduces the threshold and gain of granule cell responses to incoming mossy fiber input (Chadderton et al., 2004; Duguid et al., 2012; Mitchell and Silver, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chadderton et al., 2004; Duguid et al., 2012; Mitchell and Silver, 2003.

claim: The idea that the granule cell layer can decorrelate inputs has been supported by observations that individual granule cells can pool inputs from different sources.
source: Beyond sparsity, the idea that the granule cell layer can decorrelate inputs has also been supported by observations that individual granule cells can pool inputs from different sources (Huang et al., 2013) and with different synaptic strengths (Chabrol et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2013 and Chabrol et al., 2015.

claim: Recent work has challenged the idea that granule cells generate sparse representations, and shown that they can instead exhibit dense and redundant responses during several behaviors.
source: In contrast with classic models, recent work has challenged the idea that granule cells generate sparse representations, and shown that they can instead exhibit dense and redundant responses during several behaviors (Giovannucci et al., 2017; Knogler et al., 2017; Ozden et al., 2012; Sylvester et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Giovannucci et al., 2017; Knogler et al., 2017; Ozden et al., 2012; Sylvester et al., 2017.

claim: Pattern separation need not require sparse coding.
source: For example, pattern separation need not require sparse coding (Cayco-Gajic and Silver, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cayco-Gajic and Silver, 2019.

claim: Pattern separation can be achieved without sparse coding if inputs are still expanded and decorrelated, allowing dense granule cell responses to effectively discriminate complex, high-dimensional inputs.
source: In particular, as argued by Cayco-Gajic and Silver, pattern separation can be achieved without sparse coding if inputs are still expanded and decorrelated, allowing dense granule cell responses to effectively discriminate complex, high-dimensional inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from Cayco-Gajic and Silver, 2019.

claim: The dense granule cell responses measured thus far have been largely observed during complex behaviors where there are likely to be many sensorimotor patterns represented simultaneously.
source: It should also be noted, however, that the dense granule cell responses measured thus far have been largely observed during complex behaviors. In these cases, there are likely to be many sensorimotor patterns represented simultaneously.
evidence: This is an inference about the conditions under which dense responses have been observed.

claim: Whether the cerebellar granule cell layer acts to sparsify discrete sensorimotor inputs, and what mechanisms the granule cell layer uses to generate unique representations, remains an open question.
source: Thus, whether the cerebellar granule cell layer acts to sparsify discrete sensorimotor inputs, and what mechanisms the granule cell layer uses to generate unique representations, remains an open question.
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in the field.

claim: Previous work across many cerebellar-dependent learning paradigms had revealed considerable evidence that the granule cells encode the predictive context necessary for motor learning.
source: Previous work across many cerebellar-dependent learning paradigms had revealed considerable evidence that the granule cells encode the predictive context necessary for motor learning (Raymond and Medina, 2018; Sawtell, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raymond and Medina, 2018 and Sawtell, 2017.

claim: In associative motor learning tasks, granule cells carry information about the predictive conditioned stimulus, allowing Purkinje cells to develop learned responses to these inputs.
source: For example, in associative motor learning tasks, granule cells carry information about the predictive CS (Steinmetz et al., 1989), allowing Purkinje cells to develop learned responses to these inputs (Halverson et al., 2015; Hesslow and Ivarsson, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Steinmetz et al., 1989; Halverson et al., 2015; Hesslow and Ivarsson, 1994.

claim: For adaptation learning paradigms such as vestibulo-ocular gain learning, the granule cells receive copies of learned motor commands, or efference copies, that can provide a basis for predictive learning.
source: Likewise, for adaptation learning paradigms such as vestibulo-ocular gain learning, the granule cells receive copies of learned motor commands, or so-called efference copies, that can provide a basis for predictive learning (Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978a; Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978a and Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978b.

claim: Recent calcium imaging data further supports the idea that granule cells can represent efference copy information.
source: Indeed, recent calcium imaging data further supports the idea that granule cells can represent efference copy information (Giovannucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Giovannucci et al., 2017.

claim: Using calcium imaging to measure the responses of granule cells across eyelid conditioning, Giovannucci et al. revealed learned representations of the conditioned eyelid closure that can match, or even precede the eyelid movement after learning.
source: Using calcium imaging to measure the responses of granule cells across eyelid conditioning, Giovannucci et al. revealed learned representations of the conditioned eyelid closure that can match, or even precede the eyelid movement after learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Giovannucci et al., 2017.

claim: To establish predictive contextual representations, granule cells appear to employ population codes that take advantage of input that is tuned to specific stimulus or kinematic parameters.
source: To establish predictive contextual representations, granule cells appear to employ population codes that take advantage of input that is tuned to specific stimulus or kinematic parameters.
evidence: This is an inference about how granule cells establish representations.

claim: Elegant in vivo recordings from rodents have revealed that granule cells can be narrowly tuned to movement features such as whisker position.
source: For example, elegant in vivo recordings from rodents have revealed that granule cells can be narrowly tuned to movement features such as whisker position (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: By linearly encoding movement features according to the properties of synaptic transmission from mossy fibers, granule cells can effectively relay a population code to downstream Purkinje cells that faithfully represents precise features of upcoming movement kinematics.
source: By linearly encoding such features according to the properties of synaptic transmission from mossy fibers (Arenz et al., 2008; Duguid et al., 2012; Powell et al., 2015; Rancz et al., 2007), granule cells can effectively relay a population code to downstream Purkinje cells that faithfully represents precise features of upcoming movement kinematics (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arenz et al., 2008; Duguid et al., 2012; Powell et al., 2015; Rancz et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Predictive coding in granule cells now appears to extend beyond the motor domain, and can also reflect cognitive predictions.
source: Surprisingly, however, predictive coding in granule cells now appears to extend beyond the motor domain, and can also reflect cognitive predictions.
evidence: This is a statement about emerging evidence, supported by subsequent discussion.

claim: Using both operant and Pavlovian tasks guided by reward reinforcement, Wagner and colleagues used calcium imaging to demonstrate that granule cells can develop non-motor predictions.
source: Using both operant and Pavlovian tasks guided by reward reinforcement, Wagner and colleagues used calcium imaging to demonstrate that granule cells can develop non-motor predictions (Wagner et al., 2017; Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wagner et al., 2017 and references Figure 5.

claim: Granule cells can develop learned representations of both actions and stimuli that predict upcoming reward, with as many as 25% of the total recorded cells responding to reward, reward omission, or reward anticipation.
source: Specifically, this study revealed that granule cells can develop learned representations of both actions and stimuli that predict upcoming reward, with as many as 25% of the total recorded cells responding to reward, reward omission, or reward anticipation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Wagner et al., 2017.

claim: Population level calcium imaging in mice reveals distinct populations of granule cells that represent reward delivery, reward omission, and the anticipation of reward delivery after learning in an operant forelimb task.
source: Left, population level calcium imaging in mice reveals distinct populations of granule cells that represent reward delivery (top), reward omission (middle), and the anticipation of reward delivery (bottom) after learning in an operant forelimb task.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The same categories of granule cell responses arise following learning in a Pavlovian task where a neutral cue is associated with reward.
source: Right, the same categories of responses arise following learning in a Pavlovian task where a neutral cue (CS) is associated with reward.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: That granule cell predictions need not be exclusively related to movements is particularly exciting, and lends support to the idea that granule cells can provide a substrate for cerebellar learning that is not exclusive to motor control.
source: That such predictions need not be exclusively related to movements is particularly exciting, and lends support to the idea that granule cells can provide a substrate for cerebellar learning that is not exclusive to motor control.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of non-motor granule cell representations.

claim: If granule cell predictions are not exclusively related to movements, such predictions may be used by downstream targets in the neocortex and elsewhere for a variety of computations.
source: If so, such predictions may be used by downstream targets in the neocortex and elsewhere for a variety of computations.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential uses of non-motor granule cell representations.

claim: Several elegant studies have now begun to reveal that the sodium-based action potentials of Purkinje cells (simple spikes) can establish complex kinematic predictions about movement across diverse behaviors.
source: Several elegant studies have now begun to reveal that the sodium-based action potentials of Purkinje cells (so-called 'simple spikes') can establish complex kinematic predictions about movement across diverse behaviors (Brown and Raman, 2018; Chen et al., 2016; Ebner and Pasalar, 2008; Herzfeld et al., 2015; Pasalar et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown and Raman, 2018; Chen et al., 2016; Ebner and Pasalar, 2008; Herzfeld et al., 2015; Pasalar et al., 2006.

claim: Data showing that Purkinje cell simple spikes can establish complex kinematic predictions support the notion that the cerebellum harnesses a type of predictive computation often termed a 'forward model'.
source: Such data support the notion that the cerebellum can harnesses a type of predictive computation often termed a 'forward model'.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the data on Purkinje cell simple spikes.

claim: A forward model can be most simply conceptualized as an estimation of the immediate future based on a copy of the current motor command and current sensory information.
source: A forward model can be most simply conceptualized as an estimation of the immediate future based on a copy of the current motor command and current sensory information.
evidence: This is a definition of a forward model based on established knowledge.

claim: A key virtue of forward model predictions is that they can be used as a more rapid substitute for external feedback to enable anticipatory actions.
source: A key virtue of such predictions is that they can be used as a more rapid substitute for external feedback (e.g. the sensory consequences of movement) to enable anticipatory actions.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of forward models based on established knowledge.

claim: Forward model predictions can also be compared with subsequent sensorimotor feedback to assess differences between expectation and outcome.
source: Such forward model predictions can also be compared with subsequent sensorimotor feedback to assess differences between expectation and outcome.
evidence: This is a statement about how forward models are used based on established knowledge.

claim: When there is a mismatch between forward model predictions and sensorimotor feedback, termed a 'sensory prediction error', the forward model can be updated via learning mechanisms.
source: When there is a mismatch, termed a 'sensory prediction error', the forward model can be updated via learning mechanisms (e.g. synaptic plasticity) in accordance with current conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about how forward models are updated based on established knowledge.

claim: Climbing fiber input to Purkinje cells is typically considered to be the teaching signal necessary to update cerebellar forward models.
source: While CF input to Purkinje cells is typically considered to be the teaching signal necessary to update cerebellar forward models, there is also evidence that the granule cell pathway may carry feedback error signals (Popa and Ebner, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the classical view of cerebellar learning.

claim: There is evidence that the granule cell pathway may carry feedback error signals.
source: While CF input to Purkinje cells is typically considered to be the teaching signal necessary to update cerebellar forward models, there is also evidence that the granule cell pathway may carry feedback error signals (Popa and Ebner, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Popa and Ebner, 2018.

claim: Error signals have been observed in the simple spiking of Purkinje cells in a manner that is independent of complex spikes.
source: Such error signals have been observed in the simple spiking of Purkinje cells in a manner that is independent of Cspks (Popa et al., 2012; Popa et al., 2017; Streng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Popa et al., 2012; Popa et al., 2017; Streng et al., 2018.

claim: The observation that error signals can occur in Purkinje cell simple spiking independent of complex spikes implies that Purkinje cells can carry the necessary information for updating a cerebellar forward model without climbing fibers in some cases.
source: These data imply that Purkinje cells can carry the necessary information for updating a cerebellar forward model without CFs in some cases.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the data on error signals in simple spikes.

claim: The observation that error signals can occur in Purkinje cell simple spiking independent of complex spikes is consistent with the finding that climbing fiber activity is not required for some forms of cerebellar learning.
source: These results are also consistent with the finding that CF activity is not required for some forms of cerebellar learning (Ke et al., 2009; Kimpo et al., 2014), and may also support the idea that Cspks can serve alternate roles in some behaviors (Streng et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ke et al., 2009; Kimpo et al., 2014; Streng et al., 2017.

claim: In cases where climbing fiber activity is strongly linked to learning, the primary model suggests that these signals serve to instruct long-term synaptic depression of granule cell synapses onto Purkinje cells.
source: In cases where CF activity is strongly linked to learning, the primary model suggests that these signals serve to instruct long-term synaptic depression (LTD) of granule cell synapses onto Purkinje cells (Albus, 1971; Ito, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Albus, 1971 and Ito, 1972.

claim: The mechanism of climbing fiber-instructed long-term depression is appealing because Purkinje cells are inhibitory and exhibit high convergence onto target neurons in the cerebellar nuclei that form the output of the cerebellum.
source: This mechanism is appealing because Purkinje cells are inhibitory, and exhibit high convergence onto target neurons in the CbN that form the output of the cerebellum (Person and Raman, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Person and Raman, 2012.

claim: Predictive cerebellar output from cerebellar nuclei neurons would be greatly facilitated by an appropriately timed disinhibition that could be achieved by reducing the simple spiking of Purkinje cells.
source: Thus, predictive cerebellar output from CbN neurons would be greatly facilitated by an appropriately timed disinhibition that could be achieved by reducing the simple spiking of Purkinje cells (Heiney et al., 2014; Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heiney et al., 2014 and references Figure 6.

claim: Parallel fibers in the mossy fiber pathway carrying conditioned stimulus input are thought to be depressed when paired with climbing fiber input to Purkinje cells.
source: Parallel fibers (Figure 1) in the mossy fiber pathway carrying CS input are thought to be depressed when paired with CF input to Purkinje cells.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Depression of parallel fibers enables a well-timed reduction in Purkinje cell inhibition of cerebellar nuclei cells.
source: This enables a well-timed reduction in Purkinje cell inhibition of CbN cells.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Long-term potentiation of mossy fiber input to cerebellar nuclei cells may also facilitate learning.
source: LTP of mossy fiber input to CbN cells may also facilitate learning (Pugh and Raman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 6 and supported by a citation to Pugh and Raman, 2006.

claim: Current evidence suggests a role for plasticity of various types and at multiple sites in the cerebellar circuit.
source: Indeed, while current evidence suggests a role for plasticity of various types and at multiple sites in the cerebellar circuit (Boyden et al., 2004; Carey and Lisberger, 2002; Gao et al., 2012), there remains considerable evidence that CF-driven LTD, or at least CF-driven reductions in PC simple spiking, is involved with many forms of cerebellar learning (Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyden et al., 2004; Carey and Lisberger, 2002; Gao et al., 2012.

claim: There remains considerable evidence that climbing fiber-driven long-term depression, or at least climbing fiber-driven reductions in Purkinje cell simple spiking, is involved with many forms of cerebellar learning.
source: Indeed, while current evidence suggests a role for plasticity of various types and at multiple sites in the cerebellar circuit (Boyden et al., 2004; Carey and Lisberger, 2002; Gao et al., 2012), there remains considerable evidence that CF-driven LTD, or at least CF-driven reductions in PC simple spiking, is involved with many forms of cerebellar learning (Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ito et al., 2014.

claim: Studies of learned eye movements have provided the most direct evidence to date for a causal link between complex spike-driven reductions in Purkinje cell simple spiking and learning.
source: In particular, studies of learned eye movements have provided the most direct evidence to date for a causal link between Cspk-driven reductions in Purkinje cell simple spiking and learning (Herzfeld et al., 2018; Kimpo et al., 2014; Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2014; Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Herzfeld et al., 2018; Kimpo et al., 2014; Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2014, and references Figure 7.

claim: Studies of learned eye movements have shown that complex spikes are highly correlated with a depression of Purkinje cell simple spiking and learning on a single trial basis.
source: This work has shown that Cspks are highly correlated with a depression of PC simple spiking and learning on a single trial basis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the studies cited in the previous sentence.

claim: Studies of learned eye movements have made a key link between the duration of complex spikes and learning, revealing that these signals are graded in a manner that scales with the amount of single trial learning.
source: Moreover, these studies have made a key link between the duration of Cspks and learning, revealing that these signals are graded, likely due to graded presynaptic CF activity (Gaffield et al., 2019), in a manner that scales with the amount of single trial learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the studies cited in the previous sentence and a citation to Gaffield et al., 2019.

claim: Complex spikes on the preceding trial lead to a depression of Purkinje cell simple spiking on the next trial that is proportional to the duration of the complex spike.
source: Left, Cspks on the preceding trial lead to a depression of Purkinje cell simple spiking on the next trial that is proportional to the duration of the Cspk.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Trial over trial changes in eye velocity obey the same relationship to complex spike duration as the depression in simple spiking.
source: Right, trial over trial changes in eye velocity obey the same relationship to Cspk duration as the depression in simple spiking.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The findings from studies of learned eye movements suggest the possibility that the duration of complex spikes may be determined by behavior, with larger errors leading to longer duration or more probable climbing fiber input.
source: These findings suggest the possibility that the duration of Cspks may be also be determined by behavior, with larger errors leading to longer duration or more probable CF input (Najafi et al., 2014; Najafi and Medina, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to Najafi et al., 2014 and Najafi and Medina, 2013.

claim: Further exploring the relationship between behavioral variability, climbing fiber activity, complex spikes, and the depression of Purkinje cell simple spiking will be crucial to understanding the links between learning and its underlying mechanisms.
source: Thus, further exploring the relationship between behavioral variability (e.g. error magnitude), CF activity, Cspks, and the depression of PC simple spiking will be crucial to understanding the links between learning and its underlying mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: While considerable evidence suggests that the depression of Purkinje cell simple spiking provides at least part of the necessary substrate for predictive cerebellar output, it remains necessary to make direct links between learning and long-term depression.
source: Moreover, while considerable evidence suggests that the depression of Purkinje cell simple spiking provides at least part of the necessary substrate for predictive cerebellar output, it remains necessary to make direct links between learning and LTD.
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in the field.

claim: Conclusive tests of how long-term depression at Purkinje cell synapses contributes to learning will require manipulations that are not only cell-type specific, but also temporally specific in order to overcome the complications of circuit compensation that are inherent to chronic genetic strategies.
source: Despite key efforts in this direction (Schonewille et al., 2011; Yamaguchi et al., 2016), conclusive tests of how LTD at PC synapses contributes to learning will require manipulations that are not only cell-type specific, but also temporally specific in order to overcome the complications of circuit compensation that are inherent to chronic genetic strategies.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for future experiments, supported by citations to Schonewille et al., 2011 and Yamaguchi et al., 2016.

claim: At the level of the cerebellar nuclei, direct evidence to illustrate predictive cerebellar output has been somewhat limited.
source: At the level of the CbN, direct evidence to illustrate predictive cerebellar output has been somewhat limited.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: Clear examples of predictive cerebellar output had previously existed only for a small number motor behaviors with similar learning requirements.
source: Clear examples had previously existed only for a small number motor behaviors with similar learning requirements.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: During eyelid conditioning, cerebellar nuclei neurons become active to the conditioned stimulus to enable a predictive eyelid closure by activating downstream motor neurons.
source: For example, during eyelid conditioning, CbN neurons become active to the conditioned stimulus to enable a predictive eyelid closure by activating downstream motor neurons (McCormick and Thompson, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McCormick and Thompson, 1984.

claim: Until recently, there had been little evidence to support the idea of predictive cerebellar output during behaviors other than those that involve simple stimulus-action associations.
source: Until recently, however, there had been little evidence to support the idea of predictive cerebellar output during behaviors other than those that involve simple stimulus-action associations, and no clear neural data showing how cerebellar output might vary according to expectations associated with different sensory inputs.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: By recording from the cerebellar nuclei of awake behaving primates, Brooks and colleagues showed that these neurons can dynamically track the difference between expected motor output and sensory feedback, consistent with the computation of sensory prediction error during voluntary head movements.
source: By recording from the CbN of awake behaving primates, Brooks and colleagues showed that these neurons can dynamically track the difference between expected motor output and sensory feedback, consistent with the computation of sensory prediction error during voluntary head movements (Brooks et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brooks et al., 2015.

claim: Cerebellar nuclei neurons responded to mismatches between expected and actual head movements on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: In particular, they found that CbN neurons responded to mismatches between expected and actual head movements on a trial-by-trial basis (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Brooks et al., 2015, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Prediction-dependent cerebellar nuclei responses were continuously updated with new learning.
source: Moreover, these prediction-dependent CbN responses were continuously updated with new learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Brooks et al., 2015.

claim: The results from Brooks et al. strongly suggest that cerebellar output can reflect the computation of a prediction error that results from comparing an internal model of the sensory consequences of active head movement with actual sensory feedback.
source: These results strongly suggest that cerebellar output can reflect the computation of a prediction error that results from comparing an internal model of the sensory consequences of active head movement with actual sensory feedback.
evidence: This is an inference from the data presented in Brooks et al., 2015.

claim: The data from Brooks et al. are consistent with the forward model hypothesis, and imply that the internal model's prediction lies upstream of the cerebellar nuclei neurons, perhaps instantiated by the spiking of Purkinje cells.
source: Such data are thus consistent with the forward model hypothesis, and imply that the internal model's prediction lies upstream of the CbN neurons, perhaps instantiated by the spiking of Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the data presented in Brooks et al., 2015.

claim: Cerebellar nuclei neurons in the Brooks et al. study were modulated in the same direction regardless of the direction of sensorimotor mismatch.
source: Notably, CbN neurons in this study were modulated in the same direction regardless of the direction of sensorimotor mismatch.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings of Brooks et al., 2015.

claim: Cerebellar nuclei neurons elevated their firing regardless of whether head movement was unexpectedly restricted, or unexpectedly released from restriction during extinction learning.
source: Specifically, CbN neurons elevated their firing regardless of whether head movement was unexpectedly restricted, or unexpectedly released from restriction during extinction learning.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings of Brooks et al., 2015.

claim: Unidirectional signaling of mismatch by cerebellar nuclei neurons is likely appropriate to drive stabilizing vestibluo-spinal reflexes and to ensure stable perception that accounts for self-motion.
source: Such unidirectional signaling of mismatch is likely appropriate to drive stabilizing vestibluo-spinal reflexes (Roy and Cullen, 2001; Roy and Cullen, 2004) and to ensure stable perception that accounts for self-motion (Dale and Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to Roy and Cullen, 2001; Roy and Cullen, 2004; Dale and Cullen, 2019.

claim: Head velocity traces for a monkey making voluntary and involuntary head movements show that when force is applied from an external motor, the monkey must slowly adapt its head movement to account for the oppositional force and recover normal head velocity.
source: Top, head velocity traces for a monkey making voluntary and involuntary (imposed via rotational turntable) head movements. When force is applied from an external motor (gray interval), the monkey must slowly adapt its head movement to account for the oppositional force and recover normal head velocity.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: A representative cerebellar nuclei neuron fires only when head movement differs from expectation, and its firing rate is directly proportional to the difference between actual and expected head movement across time.
source: Middle, a representative CbN neuron fires only when head movement differs from expectation, and its firing rate is directly proportional to the difference between actual and expected head movement across time.

claim: It has remained challenging to establish causal relationships between cerebellar nuclei activity and behavior, as tools to selectively manipulate cerebellar nuclei neurons in a manner that accounts for ongoing behavior have not been available until recently.
source: It has remained challenging, however, to establish such causal relationships between CbN activity and behavior, as tools to selectively manipulate CbN neurons in a manner that accounts for ongoing behavior have not been available until recently.

claim: A recent study has used closed-loop optogenetic manipulations to alter the firing of cerebellar nuclei neurons during movement.

claim: By both activating and inhibiting cerebellar nuclei neurons at different timepoints during skilled reaching, Becker and Person revealed that the activity of these cells contributes to predictively controlling the endpoint of reaches in real time.

source: Specifically, the authors found that CbN output contributed unidirectionally to limb movement, adding velocity toward the body regardless of limb movement direction.

source: These data suggest that the cerebellum can contribute at least part of the motor command necessary to regulate ongoing movements on a millisecond timescale, calibrating behavior even during steady state performance after learning has occurred.
